The activism ran on the same clock: president of the Chicago chapter of the Negro American Labor Council; organizer who brought some 2,000 Chicagoans to the 1963 March on Washington; a participant in Martin Luther King Jr.'s Chicago Freedom Movement of 1965–66; a pioneer of the independent Black political movement who coined the phrase "plantation politics" and ran repeatedly for office himself; a member of the coalition that elected Harold Washington, Chicago's first Black mayor, in 1983; adviser to Carol Moseley Braun and mentor to the young Barack Obama as he built a South Side political base; and named plaintiff in Black v. McGuffage, the suit charging that Illinois's voting system discriminated against minority voters in the 2000 election.
He died at his Hyde Park home on October 13, 2021, survived by his wife Zenobia Johnson-Black and his daughter Ermetra.

Margaret Burroughs (November 1, 1915 – November 21, 2010) — born Victoria Margaret Taylor in St. Rose, Louisiana, and known across her working life as Margaret Taylor Goss, Margaret Taylor Goss Burroughs, and Margaret T G Burroughs — was the artist, writer, poet, educator, and arts organizer who co-founded, with her husband Charles Gordon Burroughs, the museum that became the DuSable Museum of African American History, the institution at the center of Black Chicago's cultural record.

She helped establish the South Side Community Art Center, whose opening on May 1, 1941 was dedicated by First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt; at twenty-three she was the youngest member of its board of directors.
Most of her teaching career was spent at DuSable High School, with a later professorship in humanities at Kennedy-King College (1968–1979).
